independent-variation-principle.label: Independent Variation Principle (IVP)
independent-variation-principle.definition:
For a software system S = (F, κ_F, E, Coupling, C, Γ), IVP prescribes the partition induced by the equivalence e₁ ~_Γ e₂ ⇔ Γ(e₁) = Γ(e₂): the modules of an IVP-compliant system are the Γ-equivalence classes of the element set. Four conditions make up the structural formulation.
(1) Element Admissibility: every element has at least one change driver, |Γ(e)| ≥ 1.
(2) Element Form: every element is pure (|Γ(e)| = 1) or irreducibly composite.
(3) Separation: elements with different driver assignments reside in different modules, Γ(e₁) ≠ Γ(e₂) ⇒ M(e₁) ≠ M(e₂).
(4) Unification: elements with the same driver assignment reside in the same module, Γ(e₁) = Γ(e₂) ⇒ M(e₁) = M(e₂).
independent-variation-principle.also: A driver assignment Γ(e) is the set of change drivers whose variation affects an element, not a single driver. Separation and Unification are the partition content; Admissibility and Element Form constrain the elements themselves.

change-driver.label: Change driver
change-driver.definition: A change driver γ is an equivalence class of domain conditions in the operating domain under the co-variation relation: two conditions belong to the same change driver if they are governed by the same artifact as a single amendment unit, so that revising one obligates revising the other as one change. Co-change in the artifact's revision history is only evidence that the grouping is correct; it is not what makes two conditions one driver. When the change driver's state changes, it creates a requirement for one or more elements of an engineered system to be modified. A change driver must satisfy two constitutive criteria: (1) artifact anchoring — the condition is anchored in a documentable domain artifact; (2) causal pathway — the pathway from the artifact's change to the element's required modification is step-by-step reconstructable. The finite nonempty set of change drivers is C.
change-driver.also: Denoted γ. A change driver's existence is a fact about the domain's causal structure, not a product of having been identified; no design move adds, removes, or transmutes a driver.

change-driver-assignment.label: Change-driver assignment
change-driver-assignment.definition: The assignment function Γ : E → 𝒫(C) maps each element e to its assigned change-driver set Γ(e) ⊆ C — the set of change drivers whose activation requires e to be modified. Each γ ∈ Γ(e) is established by a counterfactual test: if the artifact anchoring γ were rewritten to remove the relevant condition, would the requirement to change e disappear? Equivalently, γ ∈ Γ(e) iff e embodies at least one knowledge piece governed by γ.
change-driver-assignment.also: The causal arrow runs from domain conditions to knowledge to elements: domain conditions govern knowledge, knowledge is embodied by elements, and elements are governed by the change drivers of the knowledge they embody.

element.label: Element
element.definition: An element e ∈ E is any artifact within the system boundary — not only source code (functions, methods, classes, services) but any artifact the system comprises: configuration entries, deployment descriptors and clustering manifests, database schemas, build scripts, infrastructure definitions. The finite set of all elements is E.
element.also: Denoted e ∈ E. An element is pure when it is assigned exactly one driver, composite when more than one.

software-system.label: Software system (tuple)
software-system.definition: A software system S is a 6-tuple S = (F, κ_F, E, Coupling, C, Γ) where F is the functional purpose (the overall goal the system is designed to realize); κ_F ⊆ 𝒦_all is the relevant causal domain knowledge; E is a finite set of elements (artifacts within the system boundary that can change in response to change drivers); Coupling is the coupling relation over element pairs with a coupling dimension and strength; C is a finite set of change drivers, each associated with a knowledge slice κ_γ ⊆ κ_F partitioning κ_F; and Γ : E → 𝒫(C) is the change-driver assignment function.
software-system.also: The first components are inputs read off the domain; Γ is the pivot the principle operates on.

relevant-causal-domain-knowledge.label: Relevant causal domain knowledge
relevant-causal-domain-knowledge.definition: For a system with functional purpose F, the relevant causal domain knowledge is κ_F = {k ∈ K : k is required to realize F} — the finite set of knowledge pieces the system must embody to function correctly. It spans all concern domains required by F. Each knowledge piece k ∈ κ_F has a governing driver set Δ(k) ⊆ C: the change drivers whose activation can force k to change.
relevant-causal-domain-knowledge.also: Denoted κ_F. It is partitioned into knowledge slices, one per leaf-level change driver.

driver-independence.label: Change-driver independence
driver-independence.definition: Two change drivers γ_i and γ_j in C are independent iff γ_i ⊥ γ_j: (1) knowledge disjointness — κ_γᵢ ∩ κ_γⱼ = ∅, the knowledge slices do not overlap; and (2) activation independence — the event that γ_i activates does not logically entail that γ_j activates, and vice versa.
driver-independence.also: Driver independence is a well-formedness condition on the driver set, not a hypothesis IVP requires. Mutually coupled drivers are correctly merged into one.

driver-omission.label: Driver omission
driver-omission.definition: Failing to record a genuine change driver in C. It coarsens the optimal partition and leaves the changes that driver produces uncontained.
driver-omission.also: Omitting a driver is distinct from refinement (splitting or merging drivers), which preserves the structural results.

module.label: Module
module.definition: A module M ⊆ E is a nonempty subset of elements grouped together. The module change-driver set Γ(M) = ⋃_{e∈M} Γ(e) ⊆ C is the union of all change drivers governing the knowledge embodied by M's elements — the set of external conditions that, when they activate, force at least one element of M to change.
module.also: A modularization is a partition of the element set into modules.

modularization.label: Modularization
modularization.definition: A modularization of S is a partition 𝒫 of E into modules: every element belongs to exactly one module, and modules are disjoint. The normative decomposition is the partition P_Γ = E/⧁_Γ — the quotient set of E by the change-driver equivalence relation — the set of all change-driver-equivalence classes [e] = {e' ∈ E : Γ(e') = Γ(e)}.
modularization.also: IVP constrains the modularization through unit purity (IVP-3) and unit completeness (IVP-4).

pure-element.label: Pure element
pure-element.definition: An element e ∈ E* is pure when it is assigned exactly one change driver: |Γ(e)| = 1.
pure-element.also: Denoted e ∈ E* where |Γ(e)| = 1. A pure element is always irreducible.

irreducible-composite.label: Irreducible composite
irreducible-composite.definition: An element e* is irreducibly composite if |Γ(e*)| = n ≥ 2 and both hold: (1) purpose elimination — for every proper subset A ⊊ Γ(e*), restricting e*'s driver assignment to A eliminates the element's purpose entirely; (2) no decomposition exists — there is no partition of e* into sub-elements whose driver sets each have size < n and that jointly preserve the element's purpose.
irreducible-composite.also: Adapters and translators are typically irreducibly composite. An irreducible composite pays an intrinsic multi-driver cost forced by the domain.

coupling.label: Coupling
coupling.definition: An entity e is coupled to every other entity that accesses a resource r that e also accesses — a resource whose definition, state, or capacity e's correct behaviour depends on, and to which at least one other entity's correct behaviour also depends. A coupling is the triple (e₁, r, e₂): two entities together with the resource that links them; the resource r is the medium of the coupling.
coupling.also: Coupling is a standing constraint relation, not an event: it holds whether or not any change ever occurs.

cohesion.label: Cohesion
cohesion.definition: Cohesion is the degree to which a module complies with the partitioning rules that define its decomposition. For a system assessed under k partitioning rules 𝒫 = {R₁, …, Rₖ}, cohesion is measured by a 2k-tuple — one (purity, completeness) pair per rule. A module is fully cohesive iff it scores maximally on every component.
cohesion.also: Causal cohesion arises under the partitioning rule of change-driver-assignment identity (Γ-equivalence).

causal-cohesion.label: Causal cohesion
causal-cohesion.definition: Causal cohesion is the (purity, completeness) pair contributed by the R_Γ slot in the 2k-tuple — the component measuring fidelity to the principle of change-driver-assignment identity (k = 1). Purity (internal uniformity): every element in M shares the same change-driver-assignment set, ∀e₁,e₂∈M: Γ(e₁) = Γ(e₂). Completeness (external coverage): no element sharing M's change-driver-assignment set resides outside M, ∀e∈E: Γ(e) ∈ 𝒜(M) ⇒ e ∈ M. A module is causally cohesive iff it is both pure and complete.
causal-cohesion.also: The failure mode of impurity is accidental coupling; the failure mode of incompleteness is shotgun surgery.

cohesion-profile.label: Cohesion profile
cohesion-profile.definition: The cohesion profile of a system assessed under k partitioning rules 𝒫 = {R₁, …, Rₖ} is the 2k-tuple cohesion(M, 𝒫) = (purity₁(M,R₁), completeness₁(M,R₁), …, purityₖ(M,Rₖ), completenessₖ(M,Rₖ)) — one (purity, completeness) pair per rule, each diagnosing fidelity to that rule's partition.
cohesion-profile.also: A module is fully cohesive when it scores maximally on every component of the profile.

partitioning-rule.label: Partitioning rule
partitioning-rule.definition: A partitioning rule R is a rule that assigns every element e ∈ E to exactly one equivalence class Cᵢ ⊆ E, inducing a partition 𝒫_R = {C₁, …, Cₙ} on the element set. The assignment must satisfy four conditions — determinacy, partitionality, externality, and declarativity. A partitioning rule anchors a cohesion metric: purity and completeness are defined relative to the partition it induces.
partitioning-rule.also: The Γ-equivalence rule — group elements by identical change-driver set — is the coarsest partitioning rule that still contains every change to one module.

structural-proxy.label: Structural proxy
structural-proxy.definition: A structural measurement is any function f(e, M, 𝒫, E, R) → V whose input is restricted to structural data — the elements, the dependency relation, and the modularization — and that has no access to the principle P. Observable structural patterns of code (method-call overlap, shared-field density, connected components) correlate with cohesion but cannot define it: a structural measurement is constant on fibers of the structural projection, so it cannot distinguish correct from incorrect placement.
structural-proxy.also: Cohesion proper is correctness relative to a partitioning rule; a structural proxy cannot detect the actual failure mode.

accidental-coupling.label: Accidental coupling
accidental-coupling.definition: An accidental dependency is a dependency that exists in the implementation but is not required by any domain artifact: it lies in R ∖ R_nec. A dependency (e₁, e₂) ∈ R is required when the domain artifact grounding the class assignment of e₁ specifies that e₁ depends on e₂, and no alternative definition of e₁ that omits the reference can satisfy the domain artifact.
accidental-coupling.also: Contrast with necessary coupling, which the domain demands.

necessary-coupling.label: Necessary coupling
necessary-coupling.definition: The necessary dependency graph R_nec ⊆ R is the subset of R consisting of dependencies dictated by the domain under the partitioning principle P — the irreducible coupling floor the system cannot function without.
necessary-coupling.also: Necessary coupling is rule-relative: the same edge one concern demands internal is, under another, demanded external.

resource.label: Resource
resource.definition: A resource is anything whose definition, state, or capacity constrains the elements that share it. A resource has three components: (1) definition — what the resource is (an interface signature, a type, a schema, a pipeline configuration, a team scope, a deployment unit, a CPU allocation); (2) state — the resource's value at a point in time (the implementation behind an interface, the rows in a database, the latency budget consumed by a process); (3) capacity — the limit on concurrent or total access (API rate limits, CPU shares, memory quotas, team headcount). An element accesses a resource when its correct behaviour depends on that resource's definition, state, or capacity.
resource.also: The resource is the medium of a coupling.

visibility-principle.label: Visibility principle
visibility-principle.definition: The principle that coupling should be manifest in the toolchain: every shared resource carries an explicit contract, and violation of the contract is immediately detectable — through a compilation error, a test failure, a build break, a deployment rejection, or a runtime SLO violation.
visibility-principle.also: Reframes the classical 'minimize coupling' imperative: coupling is a standing constraint, so the goal is to make it visible and governed.

variation-dependence.label: Variation dependence
variation-dependence.definition: Two elements e₁, e₂ ∈ E are variation dependent if they share at least one change driver: Γ(e₁) ∩ Γ(e₂) ≠ ∅. The variation class of change driver γ is E_γ = {e ∈ E : γ ∈ Γ(e)} — the elements that must change when γ activates.
variation-dependence.also: Distinct from change-driver equivalence: two elements are change-driver-equivalent exactly when Γ(e₁) = Γ(e₂), which is the equivalence relation whose classes form the IVP-compliant partition.

change-driver-equivalence.label: Change-driver equivalence
change-driver-equivalence.definition: Two elements e₁, e₂ ∈ E are change-driver-equivalent, written e₁ ⧁_Γ e₂, iff Γ(e₁) = Γ(e₂). The relation ⧁_Γ is an equivalence relation on E (reflexive, symmetric, transitive), so it partitions E into change-driver-equivalence classes [e] = {e' ∈ E : Γ(e') = Γ(e)}. The set of all classes is E/⧁_Γ, the quotient set that forms the IVP-compliant partition.
change-driver-equivalence.also: Distinct from variation dependence: two elements are variation dependent when they share at least one driver (Γ(e₁) ∩ Γ(e₂) ≠ ∅); they are change-driver-equivalent exactly when their driver sets are identical.

domain.label: Domain
domain.definition: A coherent region of causal knowledge. A domain may contain multiple change drivers and decompose into subdomains; at the leaf level it contains exactly one driver.

knowledge-slice.label: Knowledge slice
knowledge-slice.definition: For a set of change drivers D ⊆ C, the knowledge slice governed by D is κ_D = {k ∈ κ_F : Δ(k) ⊆ D} — the set of all knowledge pieces whose governing change drivers are contained in D. For a single change driver γ ∈ C, κ_γ = {k ∈ κ_F : γ ∈ Δ(k)} is the knowledge slice directly governed by γ.
knowledge-slice.also: Denoted κ_γ. There is a bijection between knowledge slices and leaf-level change drivers.

unit-purity.label: Unit Purity
unit-purity.definition: IVP-3 (Separation): elements with different driver assignments belong in different modules — Γ(e₁) ≠ Γ(e₂) ⇒ M(e₁) ≠ M(e₂). Equivalently: no module contains elements with different Γ-assignments.
unit-purity.also: Also called separation of concerns formalized. The failure mode of impurity is accidental coupling.

unit-completeness.label: Unit Completeness
unit-completeness.definition: IVP-4 (Unification): elements with the same driver assignment belong in the same module — Γ(e₁) = Γ(e₂) ⇒ M(e₁) = M(e₂). Equivalently: every Γ-equivalence class is contained within a single module.
unit-completeness.also: Also called unification. The failure mode of incompleteness is shotgun surgery.

element-admissibility.label: Element Admissibility
element-admissibility.definition: IVP-1 (Admissibility): every element has at least one change driver — |Γ(e)| ≥ 1 for all e ∈ E. An element with Γ(e) = ∅ is inadmissible: it embodies no part of κ_F and falls outside the system model by definition.

change-driver-assignment-axiom.label: Change-Driver Assignment
change-driver-assignment-axiom.definition: IVP-2 (Element Form): every element is either pure (|Γ(e)| = 1) or irreducibly composite (|Γ(e)| ≥ 2 and irreducible). Reducible composites are excluded: over-broad Γ assignments are corrected upstream, and decomposable elements are split into sub-elements with strictly smaller driver assignments.

partition-theorem.label: Partition Theorem
partition-theorem.definition: The theorem that, under the objective of minimising module-touch count per change-driver activation (with non-zero contamination overhead), the partition P_Γ = E/⧁_Γ — elements grouped by identical Γ-sets — is the unique cost-minimising modularisation of a well-formed element set: no other partition achieves the same minimum. When distinct classes share a change-driver (an irreducible composite), Separation remains optimal among Separation-respecting partitions, but separating the sharing classes is globally strict only when the weighted contamination it removes exceeds the weighted shared-driver span it adds.

software-clustering.label: Software clustering
software-clustering.definition: The problem of recovering or prescribing the modular structure of a software system. Classically an NP-complete optimization over a dependency graph; given the change-driver assignment Γ, the IVP partition is computed in polynomial time.
software-clustering.also: The complexity class tracks the availability of the semantic criterion (Γ), not an intrinsic difficulty of modularisation. When Γ resists identification, structural clustering returns as a hypothesis generator, not a design criterion.

knowledge-theorem.label: Knowledge Theorem
knowledge-theorem.definition: The theorem that cohesion(M, P) = (1, 1) — a module is both pure and complete under a partitioning principle P — holds exactly when M embodies exactly the knowledge of its P-class: cohesion(M,P) = (1,1) ⟺ Knowledge(M) = K_P(Cᵢ), where K_P(Cᵢ) = ⋃_{e∈Cᵢ} Emb(e) is the knowledge embodied collectively by the elements of the P-class Cᵢ that M intersects. Maximal cohesion is maximal knowledge embodiment relative to the principle-determined knowledge grouping.
knowledge-theorem.also: Also called the knowledge-embodiment theorem. It is a result of the cohesion theory, not of IVP itself; IVP supplies one partitioning rule (change-driver identity), while the theorem concerns cohesion in general.

change-management-hypothesis.label: Change Management Hypothesis (CMH)
change-management-hypothesis.definition: The Change Management Hypothesis holds that the primary purpose of modularization is to minimize the economic cost of implementing, verifying, and maintaining the changes a system is required to undergo over its lifetime — and that architectural quality is measured by how well it achieves this. It is a normative postulate stipulating the optimisation objective that any principled modularization theory must adopt.
change-management-hypothesis.also: IVP is derived from CMH. Whether CMH is also an empirically falsifiable prediction about real maintenance costs is a separate question.

shared-resource.label: Shared resource
shared-resource.definition: The coupling medium in the shared-resource account of coupling: two entities are coupled when they both access the same resource — a resource whose definition, state, or capacity both entities' correct behaviour depends on. A coupling is the triple (e₁, r, e₂).
shared-resource.also: Formalizes coupling as a ternary (element, resource, element); Γ is derived from the resource-access and resource-governance mappings.

language-imposed-coupling.label: Language-imposed coupling
language-imposed-coupling.definition: The irreducible residuum of accidental coupling a programming language inflicts on all programs — unavoidable given the language's constructs, even under optimal design.

separation-of-concerns.label: Separation of Concerns (SoC)
separation-of-concerns.definition: The design principle that different concerns should be separated; formalized as an IVP special case when concerns correspond to change drivers.

single-responsibility-principle.label: Single Responsibility Principle (SRP)
single-responsibility-principle.definition: The heuristic, attributed to Robert Martin, that a module should have a single reason to change. Martin stated it in three formulations: SRP-1 (one reason, |Γ(M)| = 1), SRP-2 (one actor), and SRP-3 (one business function). Under IVP analysis all three mandate a singular module cardinality, and this claim is false: it makes an unsupported claim about module cardinality. An adapter between two independently governed drivers has |Γ(M)| = 2 and is irreducibly composite — no decomposition into sub-elements with |Γ(eᵢ)| < 2 preserves its purpose — so it violates all three formulations yet cannot be split.

open-closed-principle.label: Open/Closed Principle (OCP)
open-closed-principle.definition: The heuristic that software should be open for extension but closed for modification. Analyzed by IVP as a change-driver consequence under driver hierarchy.

dependency-inversion-principle.label: Dependency Inversion Principle (DIP)
dependency-inversion-principle.definition: The heuristic that high-level modules should not depend on low-level modules; both should depend on abstractions. Under IVP analysis, DIP changes the placement of a dependency: it relocates the change-propagation boundary onto the abstraction's contract. DIP does not add, remove, or transmute a change driver, and it does not reduce the change-propagation blast radius of any engaged driver — it repositions the boundary the driver propagates across.

liskov-substitution-principle.label: Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP)
liskov-substitution-principle.definition: The behavioral contract principle that subtypes must be substitutable for their base types. Analyzed by IVP through behavioral contracts and variation independence.

interface-segregation-principle.label: Interface Segregation Principle (ISP)
interface-segregation-principle.definition: The heuristic that clients should not be forced to depend on interfaces they do not use. Under IVP, ISP is a conditional corollary of DIP applied per client.

grasp.label: GRASP
grasp.definition: Larman's set of nine responsibility-assignment patterns (Information Expert, Creator, Low Coupling, High Cohesion, and others). Under IVP analysis they reduce to one unresolved coupling–cohesion tension.

paradigm.label: Programming paradigm
paradigm.definition: A style or family of languages (object-oriented, functional, procedural, dynamic) that realizes principles through specific constructs; paradigms implement principles rather than define them.
